transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-10
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~56 minutes
Attendees: Jenna Park (Redwood AE), Carlos Mendes (Redwood SE), Mark Li (Nimbus Head of ML), Sofia Alvarez (Nimbus Platform Eng), Priya Singh (Nimbus Product)

Summary: Quick POC scoping to align on latency SLOs (TTFT vs TPOT), define p95/p99 targets for short chat vs long completions, agree on measurement plan and timeline for baseline runs. Action items and next steps captured at the end.

Topics: TTFT (Time to first token) vs TPOT (time per output token), p95/p99 targets, concurrency and warm-up, synthetic vs production replay, measurement harness, KV cache/priming, model variants, dedicated vs hosted considerations.

00:00 Jenna: hey everyone thanks for hopping on. quick intros before we dig in, i'm jenn a redwood account exec.
00:10 Mark: hi, i'm mark, head of ml at nimbus. we own the recommendation and chat pipelines.
00:14 Sofia: sofia, platform eng, i'll help run the tests and provide traffic traces.
00:17 Priya: priya from product, interested in latency and UX implications.
00:22 Carlos: carlos, se at redwood, i'll own the benchmark harness and ops questions.
00:30 Jenna: high level goal — nimbus wants a 6–8 week POC to validate that redwood can meet our latency SLOs and consistent throughput under expected traffic patterns.
00:45 Mark: yes exactly. we have two primary workloads: short chat messages (avg token output ~8 tokens) and document completion where outputs are longer (~200 tokens). we care about both TTFT and per-token speed.
01:05 Carlos: ok we typically define TTFT as time from request acceptance to first token emitted. TPOT in our convo here we'll treat as time per output token (ms/token) or equivalently throughput in tokens/sec. does that match your understanding?
01:21 Mark: yes. we sometimes call it per-token latency; fine.
01:25 Priya: quick question — what are the sample p95/p99 numbers you usually see for hosted vs dedicated? just ballpark.
01:32 Carlos: ballpark: on hosted with small models p95 TTFT can be in the 120–250ms range for short generations; p99 300–600ms depending on cold starts and queuing. TPOT varies by model & hardware, around 5–40 ms/token on modern GPU for medium models; dedicated optimized infra can tighten those. but important to measure under your actual sequence lengths and concurrency.
02:00 Mark: our SLO target proposal — short chat: p95 TTFT <= 200ms, p99 <= 400ms; TPOT p95 <= 20ms/token, p99 <= 40ms/token. For long completions, p95 TTFT <= 400ms (we're less strict), TPOT p95 <= 25ms/token. Thoughts?
02:25 Carlos: those are reasonable starting targets. we'll want to bucket by sequence length and concurrency. also KV cache priming will heavily affect TTFT for repeated contexts (hot prompts).
02:40 Sofia: so for our benchmarking we can provide a traffic trace broken out by message length and by % of repeat contexts (we see ~35% of chats hit cacheable prefixes).
02:52 Jenna: good — we'll make sure the measurement plan includes a cache-primed scenario and a cold-start scenario.
03:00 Carlos: measurement plan outline: 1) baseline single-request latency profile (cold and warm) across representative models; 2) scaled concurrency tests with your expected QPS and spikes; 3) long-run stability (1–2 hour run) to observe tail behavior and memory leakage; 4) regression tests comparing model variants (quantized vs fp16) and dedicated vs hosted profiles.
03:28 Mark: sounds good. for scaled tests our peak expected qps for chat is 120 rps, typical steady 40 rps. long completion workload peaks at 6–8 rps.
03:44 Carlos: ok we'll design the load generator to replay your trace with those qps and with the same seq-length distributions. we'll also instrument to measure TTFT, TPOT, latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99), tokens/sec, and error rates.
04:03 Priya: what about measurement location — do you measure at the client side or measure at the runtime? we need user-perceived latency.
04:11 Carlos: we'll capture both. client-side (end-to-end) with synthetic users will give user-perceived TTFT, while server-side traces will let us attribute latency to network, routing, model runtime, and queuing. we'll correlate them.
04:26 Mark: good. how do we treat streaming vs non-streaming? our chat is streaming first-token then tokens.
04:33 Carlos: streaming is crucial — TTFT is first-token emission for streaming requests. For non-streaming completions we measure time-to-last-token as well. we'll include both metrics.
04:45 Jenna: example SLO buckets we'll propose in the template: short-chat (<= 32 tokens expected output), mid (33–128), long (>128). each bucket gets p95/p99 TTFT and TPOT targets.
04:58 Mark: ok that bucket map aligns with our product buckets.
05:05 Sofia: we run in aws eu-west-1 and have a private VPC setup. can you run the POC in a private deployment or needs hosted?
05:15 Carlos: we can run in Redwood Private (VPC) for the POC to mimic your network path; hosted also possible but private will give more realistic latencies. dedicated capacity can be provisioned for the benchmark window to avoid noisy neighbors.
05:33 Mark: we prefer private to remove variability. is there extra setup time?
05:37 Jenna: setup for a private POC usually takes 1–2 weeks to provision, network peering and KMS exchange included. that fits our 6–8 week window.
05:50 Priya: any security hurdles? we need SOC2 docs and for keys we use a customer-managed KMS.
05:58 Jenna: we'll send our SOC2 summary and KMS integration guide after the call.
06:05 Carlos: back to SLOs — for tail behavior we recommend measuring p99 over 30-minute windows and reporting rolling p99; p99 spikes during short windows are expected during cold starts so we'll track cold vs warm separately.
06:22 Mark: when you say cold start, is that model load or cache cold?
06:26 Carlos: both. cold can mean model instance spin-up (if not warm), cache cold (KV not primed), or client TCP/HTTP warm-up. we'll define cold windows as the first 60 seconds after scale-up in the run.
06:38 Mark: ok. we want the POC to demonstrate stable warm behavior — warm p95 TTFT <= 200ms for chat.
06:46 Carlos: noted. for throughput tests we'll also measure sustained tokens/sec under concurrency, and per-instance throughput so you can extrapolate capacity.
06:56 Priya: how do you handle batching? does batching increase TTFT?
07:00 Carlos: yes batching trades latency for throughput. our runtime supports adaptive batching — we'll test with batching off and then with production-like batching policies. we'll capture the effect on TTFT and TPOT so you can choose.
07:18 Mark: worth noting we currently enforce 300ms UI threshold for first token in chat; if TTFT exceeds that we'll consider it a fail. so the p99 threshold can't be above 300ms for our user acceptance.
07:31 Jenna: ok let's capture that as a hard check in success criteria (p99 TTFT for short-chat <= 300ms).
07:39 Carlos: good. for p95 and p99 values we'll propose the following initial SLOs in the template (short-chat): p95 TTFT <= 200ms, p99 TTFT <= 300ms; TPOT p95 <= 20ms/token, p99 <= 40ms/token. for long completions: p95 TTFT <= 400ms, p99 <= 700ms, TPOT p95 <= 25ms/token.
08:03 Mark: that matches earlier. question on measurement: how do we handle variable sequence lengths affecting TPOT? we want medians across buckets not averaged over long tails.
08:13 Carlos: we'll bucket by expected output length and report TPOT per bucket. also report tokens/sec per concurrent request and per second for the system.
08:22 Priya: what about distribution of concurrency per user? our app multiplexes several calls per user session — should we simulate that?
08:29 Sofia: yes we can provide session traces that show multiplexing and our client-level concurrency; i'll include that in the traffic trace.
08:35 Carlos: great — we'll support session-level replay in the harness, it's important for realistic queueing behavior.
08:43 Jenna: timeline recap: Jenna sends SLO doc + template by Friday (2026-03-12). Nimbus provides trace + dataset by Mon (2026-03-16). Carlos will stage harness and run initial baseline week of Mar 23. Then we run dedicated private benchmark the following week.
08:59 Mark: ok. are you planning to run baseline on the same model variants we currently use? we listed t5-like and a larger decoder model in our pre-call doc.
09:07 Carlos: yes we'll run both models and also try a quantized variant if you want to evaluate cost/latency tradeoffs. please confirm which model versions you want in the trace.
09:17 Mark: i'll confirm in the action items.
09:20 Priya: when you run the benchmark can you also capture cost estimates (per-1M tokens) for each config? product would like cost vs latency curves.
09:28 Carlos: we'll include cost modelling for each run — tokens processed, instance-hours, and approximate $/1M tokens based on the dedicated config.
09:36 Mark: good. what about p99 SLA windows? we may want rolling 30m p99 <= 400ms as an operational target.
09:44 Carlos: we'll surface rolling-window p99 metrics and also longer-term percentiles for the run.
09:50 Jenna: any blockers for starting? seems we have the items. sofia — can you confirm who will own dataset upload and temporary S3 bucket?
09:58 Sofia: yes i'll own that, i'll send details in the action item.
10:02 Mark: one more question — how do you account for network variance in eu-west-1? our clients are global but main users in eu.
10:11 Carlos: we'll run tests from aws eu-west-1 as you host, and also from a few client-side vantage points to estimate network delta. we'll report both.
10:20 Priya: ok. let me call out acceptance criteria we want in final POC report: 1) meets p99 TTFT <= 300ms for short-chat across peak load; 2) p95 TPOT <= 20ms/token for chat; 3) stable error rate <0.1%; 4) cost within x% of projected target (we'll fill x once we see cost model).
10:44 Jenna: we'll include that list in the SLO doc for sign-off.
10:48 Carlos: measuring error rate — we'll also track decoding errors, OOMs, and any retry/requeue events.
10:53 Mark: good.
11:00 [brief audio glitch at 11:00 — one second drop]
11:05 Carlos: ok moving on to benchmark specifics — warm-up policy: 5 minutes steady traffic to populate KV cache and spin instances, then test phases: ramp, steady-state 20–30 minutes, and spike tests (burst 2–3x).
11:25 Sofia: that works. should we seed the cache with common prefixes? we have the top 500 prompts.
11:30 Carlos: yes please include the top 500 prompts to seed cache scenario. we'll run seeded and unseeded runs.
11:36 Mark: also curious if you can demonstrate graceful degradation — if capacity is constrained do you fall back to lower-cost model automatically?
11:43 Jenna: yes we can simulate routed fallback policies in the test, show failover to a smaller model and measure user impact.
11:50 Priya: will that be part of core acceptance or optional?
11:53 Mark: optional but desirable.
12:00 Carlos: instrumentation — we'll push logs and metrics to a shared prometheus/grafana instance you provide or we'll ship a read-only dashboard link. for the POC we usually provide a temporary dashboard link.
12:12 Sofia: temporary dashboard fine. we prefer not to open write permissions into our cluster.
12:18 Carlos: understood. we'll provide dashboards and CSV exports of raw latency traces.
12:24 Jenna: ok last quick topic — can we include a short tech deep-dive after the baseline to discuss kernel selection and quantization tradeoffs?
12:33 Carlos: yes, we'll do a 60-minute deep-dive after baseline results are in.
12:38 Mark: sounds good.
12:41 Jenna: recap of next steps and owners — will follow up with calendar invites. any other questions?
12:48 Priya: none here.
12:50 Mark: no, thanks everyone.
12:54 Jenna: thanks — talk soon.

Post-call notes:
- We agreed on SLO buckets and initial targets: short-chat p95 TTFT <= 200ms, p99 TTFT <= 300ms; TPOT p95 <= 20ms/token, p99 <= 40ms/token. Long completions more lenient.
- Measurement plan includes cold/warm windows, cache-primed vs unprimed runs, concurrency and spike testing, and rolling p99 windows.
- Timeline: SLO doc by 2026-03-12; trace + dataset by 2026-03-16; baseline runs week of 2026-03-23; dedicated private benchmark following week.
- Deliverables: SLO/measurement template (Jenna), harness and test plan (Carlos), traffic traces and dataset (Sofia), POC acceptance criteria finalized by Mark.

References mentioned: SLO template link: https://redwood.app/slo-template (placeholder), benchmark harness repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/benchmarks (placeholder), SOC2 summary: link to be shared.
